scenes.heading: Rational and irrational numbers
scenes.sub: Can every number be written as a fraction?
scenes.say: Point seven five is three quarters. Point three recurring is one third. But can every number be written as a fraction? Today you'll meet the numbers that can't.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Cover a length with identical tiles: no gaps, no cutting
scenes.science: Rational lengths fit some tile size exactly; √2 never does
scenes.breaks: Real tiles and measurements are never perfectly exact, so this only works in the perfect world of maths.
scenes.say: Imagine covering a length with identical tiles, with no gaps and no cutting. You can pick any tile size. Every rational length fits some tile size exactly. But a length like root two never fits: however tiny the tiles, there's always a gap or an overlap.
scenes.caption: Imagine covering a length with identical tiles, no gaps and no cutting. You can pick any tile size. Every rational length fits some tile size exactly. But a length like √2 never fits.

scenes.heading: Rational or irrational?
scenes.say: Rational numbers can be written as a fraction of integers. That includes integers, terminating decimals and recurring decimals. Irrational numbers never end and never repeat, like pi, root two, and other surds. Careful: root sixteen is four, so it's rational.

scenes.heading: The real numbers
notes: Fractions and repeating decimals are rational
scenes.say: Here's the whole family. Every real number is either rational or irrational. Integers like minus four and seven sit inside the rationals, along with fractions and decimals that stop or repeat. Surds like root two, and pi, live in the irrational box.

scenes.heading: Recurring decimal to fraction
scenes.question: Write 0.4̇5̇ as a fraction.
scenes.say: Let's turn point four five recurring into a fraction. Call it x. Two digits repeat, so multiply by one hundred: one hundred x is forty-five point four five four five. Subtract, and the endless tails cancel: ninety-nine x equals forty-five. So x is forty-five ninety-ninths, which simplifies to five elevenths.
scenes.caption: Turn 0.4̇5̇ into a fraction. Call it x. Two digits repeat, so multiply by 100: 100x = 45.4545… Subtract and the tails cancel: 99x = 45. So x = 45/99 = 5/11.

scenes.heading: Only one digit repeats
scenes.question: Write 0.16̇ as a fraction.
scenes.say: Now point one six, where only the six repeats. Ten x is one point six six six, and one hundred x is sixteen point six six six. Both have the same tail. Subtract: ninety x equals fifteen. So x is fifteen ninetieths, which is one sixth.
scenes.caption: Now 0.16̇, where only the 6 repeats. 10x = 1.666… and 100x = 16.666… Both have the same tail. Subtract: 90x = 15. So x = 15/90 = 1/6.

scenes.heading: Estimating a surd
scenes.question: Between which two whole numbers is √30?
scenes.say: Root thirty isn't a whole number, but you can estimate it. Five squared is twenty-five and six squared is thirty-six. Thirty is between them, so root thirty is between five and six, a bit closer to five. It's about five point four eight.
scenes.caption: √30 isn't a whole number, but you can estimate it. 5² = 25 and 6² = 36. 30 is between them, so √30 is between 5 and 6, a bit closer to 5. It's about 5.48.

scenes.heading: Where is root thirty?
scenes.say: On the number line, root thirty sits between five and six, just to the left of five and a half.
scenes.caption: √30 sits between 5 and 6, just to the left of 5.5.

scenes.say: Quick recap. Rational numbers can be written as a fraction of integers. If a decimal stops or repeats, it's rational. Pi and surds are irrational. To turn a recurring decimal into a fraction, multiply and subtract. And estimate square roots using the square numbers on either side. Now try the practice questions!
